sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Stability Ball Shoulder Press is a dumbbell overhead press performed while seated on a stability ball.

By replacing the bench with a stability ball, this exercise adds an unstable surface that challenges your core, stabilising muscles, and balance while simultaneously building shoulder strength.

This exercise is popular in functional training, rehabilitation programmes, and general fitness routines as it develops both upper-body strength and whole-body stability.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Builds shoulder strength through a full overhead pressing range of motion
- Engages the core intensely due to the unstable surface of the stability ball
- Improves balance and proprioception
- Activates stabilising muscles of the spine, hips, and lower body
- Suitable for all fitness levels with adjustable dumbbell weight
- Promotes good posture and shoulder mobility
- A functional alternative to a seated shoulder press on a fixed bench

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Deltoids (Anterior, Medial, and Posterior heads), Upper Trapezius

Secondary: Triceps, Serratus Anterior, Core (Rectus Abdominis, Obliques, Transverse Abdominis), Glutes and Legs (active as stabilisers)

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Select a pair of dumbbells at an appropriate weight.
2. Sit on a stability ball with your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
3. Hold the dumbbells at shoulder level with your palms facing forward and elbows bent, pointing out to the sides.
4. Sit tall with your chest up, core engaged, and spine in a neutral position.
5. Ensure your hips and knees are at approximately 90 degrees.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Brace your core to stabilise your position on the ball.
2. Press the dumbbells upward toward the ceiling in a smooth, controlled arc, extending your arms fully without locking out your elbows.
3. At the top of the movement, your arms should be roughly vertical and your biceps near your ears.
4. Slowly lower the dumbbells back down to shoulder level, keeping your elbows at approximately 90 degrees.
5. Maintain a stable, upright torso on the ball throughout the entire movement.
6. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Arching the lower back excessively during the press
- Allowing the hips to sag or the ball to shift
- Using momentum rather than controlled muscle contraction
- Locking out the elbows at the top of the movement
- Feet too close together, reducing balance on the ball
- Letting the core disengage mid-set
- Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears at the top of the press

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- A pair of Dumbbells (select a weight appropriate for overhead pressing)
- Stability Ball (sized so that hips and knees are at approximately 90 degrees when seated)
- Clear floor space with no obstacles nearby in case of balance loss
- Optional: Exercise mat placed under or around the ball for safety

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Ball Size
sections.content:
1. When seated, your thighs should be parallel to the floor or angled very slightly downward.
2. A 55 cm ball is typically suitable for people 5'1" to 5'7" (155–170 cm).
3. A 65 cm ball suits those 5'8" to 6'1" (173–185 cm).
4. A 75 cm ball is generally for those over 6'1" (185+ cm).
5. Ensure the ball is properly inflated — it should compress slightly under your weight but remain firm.
6. Always check the ball for damage or slow leaks before use.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Feet: Flat on the floor, hip-width or slightly wider for better stability.
2. Hips: Centred on the ball, sitting tall and evenly balanced.
3. Core: Actively braced throughout the entire exercise.
4. Back: Neutral spine — avoid rounding or hyperextending.
5. Dumbbells: Held at shoulder height with elbows bent at about 90 degrees.
6. Grip: Palms facing forward or at a slight angle — whichever feels most comfortable for your shoulder joint.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press: Same pressing movement on a fixed bench — useful for heavier loads
- Barbell Overhead Press: Standing barbell variation for maximum strength development
- Arnold Press: Dumbbell press with a rotational component for greater deltoid activation
- Cable Shoulder Press: Constant tension through the range of motion
- Landmine Press: Shoulder-friendly angled pressing variation

sections.heading: Stability Ball Variations
sections.content:
Stability Ball Shoulder Press: Standard seated overhead press on the ball
Single-Arm Stability Ball Shoulder Press: Unilateral variation for greater core challenge
Stability Ball Push Press: Add a slight leg drive for a power component
Stability Ball Neutral Grip Press: Palms facing each other for a shoulder-friendly variation
Stability Ball Alternating Press: Press one arm at a time for added anti-rotation core demand

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Shoulder Pain: Try a neutral grip or reduce the range of motion; consult a physiotherapist
Balance Difficulty: Start with a wider foot stance or choose a fixed bench until confidence increases
Lower Back Discomfort: Ensure core is braced and avoid hyperextension; consider standing variations
No Stability Ball: Use a flat bench or adjustable bench set to 90 degrees
Beginner: Start with lighter dumbbells to master form and balance before progressing weight
